scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Her behavior reinforces an unhealthy dynamic where you’re expected to bear the brunt of household labor while she sits idle. - **Alternative Approach:** If she’s struggling with stress (common during pandemics), she might need support, not blame. But her refusal to cook *while* expecting you to do it is the real issue. --- ### **4. Is it AITA for refusing to cook today?** **No, but with nuance.** - **You’re not wrong for prioritizing your work.** If she’s not contributing, you’re not obligated to fill the gap forever. - **But:** If you want to avoid conflict, consider: - **Negotiating:** "I can’t cook every night, but I’ll help with [X] if you handle [Y]." - **Setting Boundaries:** "I need 2 hours for homework before dinner. Can we plan meals in advance?" - **Involving Your Dad:** He’s clearly overburdened. Maybe he can mediate or take on more cooking/chores. - **Long-Term:** If she continues to expect you to cook without reciprocity, you’re being taken advantage of. It’s okay to push back—especially as an adult (even if you’re still in high school). --- ### **5. What’s the bigger picture?** This scenario highlights **systemic gender/parenting imbalances** that often go unchecked: - **Unequal Labor:** Your dad does most of the cooking/chores, while your mom watches TV. This is a common (and unfair) dynamic in many households. - **Childhood vs. Adulthood:** You’re being treated like a child (expected to cook without pay) while she acts like a lazy adult. That’s not fair. - **Pandemic Stress:** If she’s overwhelmed, she should ask for help, not dump the burden on you. --- ### **Suggested Next Steps:** 1. **Have a calm, structured conversation:** - *"Mom, I love helping, but I’m really struggling with schoolwork now. Can we figure out a way to share dinner duties? Maybe you cook 3 nights a week, and I’ll handle the rest when I can?"* - If she resists: *"I understand you’re busy, but Dad does most of the cooking/chores. Can we all pitch in more fairly?"* 2. **Document the imbalance:** - Keep a log of who does what (e.g., "Dad cooks 5x/week, Mom does 0x, I do 2x"). This can help you (or your dad) advocate for change later. 3. **Protect your mental health:** - If she continues to shame you, consider: - Talking to your dad about the unfairness. - Setting a limit (e.g., "I’ll cook once a week unless you help with the rest"). - Seeking support from a school counselor or trusted adult if the conflict escalates. 4. **Model fairness:** - If you’re a good cook, offer to teach her simple meals (e.g., one-pot dishes) or help her find recipes. But don’t enable her avoidance. --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re not wrong for refusing to cook today. **The real issue is the unfairness of the system.** If your mom can’t or won’t contribute, she should adjust her expectations—not dump them on you. Your dad’s role as the primary cook/chore-doer is unsustainable, and this dynamic needs to change. Would you like help drafting a script for talking to her? Or strategies for handling her reactions?
